newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi Kurds gird for renewed war.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurds gird for renewed war.

text.p: Iraqi Kurds are girding for civil war, convinced that fierce fighting in Arbil last week marked the resumption of a long-running conflict that has also set Iraq, Iran and the United States on a collision course.
"The fire in Arbil will spread to other places," said 58-year-old Abbas, a taxi driver still shaken by the sight of Iraqi tanks in his city last weekend.
"We are cursed," he said. "We fight among ourselves, always. Outsiders help us, urge us, so we are fighting their battles, too. Peace for us is like war in other places."

When Kurdish warlord Massoud Barzani invited Saddam Hussein to help him recapture Arbil from rival troops led by Jalal Talabani and backed by Iran, an obscure 30-year-old feud suddenly rocked world capitals.

Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), relying on Iraqi tanks and artillery, won the city in a few hours of fighting and sent the peshmerga guerrillas of Talabani's Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) scurrying eastward.

The fight between Barzani and Talabani, which has simmered off and on for decades, now seems headed for a showdown over control of Kurdish northern Iraq and the big "tax" revenues from Turkish border traders and smugglers.
Barzani told reporters on Wednesday he anticipated a major counter-attack by Talabani's forces, perhaps around Arbil.
PUK supporters reckon Barzani will try to maintain the offensive by driving Talabani and his soldiers into Iran, effectively cementing KDP control over Iraqi Kurdistan.

This latest chapter in the Barzani-Talabani feud might warrant little more than than a footnote in the history of a tempestuous region, were Iraq and Iran not involved in what so far remains largely a proxy fight, with the United States trying to use the Kurds to contain both.
"How many scorpions can the U.S. squeeze into one bottle?" asked a western aid worker in Arbil.

Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's incursion into Arbil, at Barzani's request, brought a hail of U.S. cruise missiles on his air defence system and may have cost him an oil-for-food deal he had been negotiating with the United Nations.
But the Baghdad government does not appear to have been a big loser. Saddam rallied his people with defiant military rhetoric in defence of his country's territorial integrity.
It is U.S. policy in northern Iraq, born of the inconclusive end to the 1991 Gulf War, which threatens to unravel altogether.
Humanitarian in origin, the U.S.-enforced safe haven in the the Iraqi north kept the Kurds alive but stranded in a dreary no-man's land of severely limited horizons.
Barzani, who knows through bitter experience that the Kurds are pawns in a far larger game, has clearly grown restless with what he sees as a the drift and inattention of U.S. policy.

He told reporters that repeated warnings to the United States that Talabani's fighters -- backed by Iran -- were about to attack, as they did on August 17, went unanswered and that the KDP was left with no alternative but to fend for itself.
"If they (the United States) do not protect us we are obliged to protect ourselves," he told reporters on Wednesday in his stronghold of Salahuddin.
"It is true we are a poor people and we cannot do a lot of things. They (the United States) are a big country and they run the world. But when they give a commitment they should keep it."
There is a new militancy to Barzani, who has often been criticised by his own lieutenants for compromising with Talabani and trying to work out their differences peacefully.

The KDP won a narrow victory in Kurdish elections in northern Iraq in May of 1992. In a gesture of reconciliation Barzani gave one of his parliamentary seats to the PUK, so they could enter the new legislative assembly with equal shares of power.
Barzani now broods over that move, which he says Talabani exploited to finally seize Arbil in 1994, banishing the KDP from the seat of the parliament and the capital of northern Iraq.
"I regret it because we made some concessions to avoid fighting and we failed," he said.
"It would have been better to have the fighting then because it would have been clear the battle was between legitimacy and dictatorship. Now the matter has been muddled."
